raw:
{
  "need": "Competence",
  "secondary": { "name": "Identity" },
  "read": "This student put in real effort and still came up short, which scrambles their internal logic: if trying hard did not work, the only explanation that makes sense to them is a fixed ceiling on their ability. That conclusion protects their sense of dignity — it is safer to be bad at something than to be someone who tried and still failed. The identity thread is right underneath: they are starting to write 'not a math person' or 'not a science person' into their self-story, and once that label sticks it governs every future choice.",
  "pull": { "collapse": "Protector", "instinct": "Say something like 'You did great just for trying, the test was hard' — which feels kind but quietly confirms that the result was the ceiling, letting them off the hook and giving up on them without admitting it." },
  "mentorMove": "Hold the standard by taking the effort seriously — not dismissing it — while reframing the result as information about the strategy, not a verdict on the person. Make it clear you expect them to get there and that you will work alongside them to find a path that matches how their brain is actually processing this material.",
  "holdFirm": [
    "The standard for what understanding this material looks like does not move.",
    "You keep treating the student as someone who is building capability, not someone who has been sorted into a lower category."
  ],
  "stayFlexible": [
    "How they practice between now and the next attempt is open — worked examples, a study group, office time, a different set of problems, whatever gets traction.",
    "How you give feedback can flex: written notes on their work, a quick verbal debrief, or walking through one problem together — whatever they are most willing to engage with right now."
  ],
  "forceLevel": { "level": 2, "label": "Questions" },
  "script": [
    { "phase": "Connection", "words": "Hey, I saw your score and I also know you put time into this one. I want to talk about it for two minutes if that is okay." },
    { "phase": "Curiosity", "words": "When you were studying, what did that actually look like — like, what were you doing? I am asking for real because I want to figure out where things got slippery, not just tell you to study more." },
    { "phase": "Collaboration", "words": "Here is what I think I am seeing: the effort was real, but the approach and the way the test asked the questions did not line up yet. That is a strategy gap, not a talent gap, and strategy is something we can actually fix. What part of the material felt shakiest when you were in the middle of the test?" },
    { "phase": "Commitment", "words": "I am holding you to actually understanding this, not just moving past it, because I have high standards for you and I genuinely believe you can get there — I have seen what you do when something clicks. Let us pick one thing to try differently before the next assessment and see if it moves the needle." }
  ],
  "longGame": "Every time this student studies hard and the result improves even a little, name it specifically and connect it back to the strategy shift, not to innate ability. Over several cycles, you are replacing a fixed-ability story with a track record of evidence that effort plus better method equals growth — and that track record becomes the new identity they carry forward."
}
situation: A student who clearly studied did poorly and is convinced they are just bad at this subject.
